title: Lutherans and the Reformed
hook: Lutherans kept much liturgy; Calvin's Reformed churches stressed God's sovereignty and scripture

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Reformation: a monk, ninety-five theses, and one line from Ephesians. Your line was by grace through faith. What did you catch yourself trying to earn? Day two hundred ninety.

Walk into two Protestant churches from the 1600s. The first is a Lutheran church in Germany. There's an altar with candles, a crucifix, maybe painted panels, a pastor in robes, and up in the balcony an organ roaring out a hymn the whole congregation knows by heart. Johann Sebastian Bach will one day write music for churches like this. The second is a Reformed church in the Netherlands or Scotland. The walls are whitewashed. No statues, no pictures. In the center, instead of an altar, a tall pulpit, and on it an open Bible. The people sing psalms, plainly. It's so bare your eye has nowhere to go but the pulpit. Both came out of the same Reformation, just a few years apart. Today's word is the two families that grew from it.
screen: `CANDLES, CRUCIFIX, AN ORGAN.` → `WHITE WALLS, A PULPIT, A BIBLE.` → `SAME REFORMATION, TWO ROOMS.`

segments.voice: Lutherans follow Martin Luther. His rule of thumb was this: keep whatever in the old worship the Bible doesn't forbid. So Lutherans kept much of the liturgy, the church year, vestments, candles, and they poured their faith into music. Bach, a Lutheran, often wrote three letters at the end of his scores: S.D.G., soli Deo gloria, to God alone the glory. The Reformed tradition comes from Swiss reformers, Ulrich Zwingli in Zurich and, above all, John Calvin in Geneva. Their rule of thumb went further: in worship, keep what scripture calls for, and let the rest go. Hence the white walls. From Geneva, the Reformed faith spread to Scotland, where John Knox founded what became the Presbyterian church, to the Netherlands, Hungary, and later New England. At its center is the sovereignty of God: God is king over everything, every life, every hour, and salvation is God's work from start to finish. A catechism written in 1647 for Reformed churches in England and Scotland opens with a famous question and answer: "What is the chief end of man? Man's chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever." Notice the second half. Enjoy. The two families agreed on almost everything, grace, faith, scripture, but split over communion. At a meeting in Marburg in 1529, Luther and Zwingli agreed on fourteen points out of fifteen. The fifteenth was the Lord's Supper. Luther held that Christ's body is truly present in the bread; Zwingli saw it as a memorial; Calvin later taught a real but spiritual presence. They couldn't agree, and parted. Nearly five centuries later, many Lutheran and Reformed churches signed agreements that put them in full communion, in Europe in 1973 and in the United States in 1997.
screen: `LUTHERANS: KEEP WHAT ISN'T FORBIDDEN.` · `REFORMED: KEEP WHAT SCRIPTURE CALLS FOR.` · `GOD IS KING OVER EVERYTHING.` · `MARBURG: FOURTEEN OF FIFTEEN.` · then, large: `TO GLORIFY GOD, AND TO ENJOY HIM FOR EVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice something simple and beautiful. If you can, picture a church you know: a candle, a window, a plain wooden table, an open Bible. If you're not near a church, look around the room you're in. Find one simple thing that is beautiful exactly as it is. Settle, and breathe. Let it be enough. If you pray, you can give it back with Bach's three letters: to God alone the glory. If you don't, just enjoy it. The catechism would say that counts too. The bell holds the time.
Lutherans and the Reformed. The two first families of the Reformation: Luther's, with its liturgy and music, and Calvin's, with its plain walls and God's sovereignty.
Your line: god is sovereign. Today, when something is out of your control, notice it, and let it be held by someone bigger. Day two hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Lutheran churches usually worship with a set liturgy, hymns and weekly or frequent communion; Reformed and Presbyterian churches center worship on the reading and preaching of scripture, often in plain sanctuaries.
